props.title: Anatomy of a Workflow
props.sub: one YAML file, line by line

props.title: Fifteen lines that test every change

notes.t: name — the label shown in the Actions tab
on — the trigger: pushes to main + every pull request
steps — checkout, install Node, install deps, test

captions: Part two. Anatomy of a workflow.
Let's open a real workflow file and read it,
line by line.
Workflows live in one place: a folder called dot
github, slash workflows. Any YAML file there is a
workflow.
Line one, name, is just the label you'll see
in the UI.
Next, on. This is the trigger. Here: run on
every push to main, and on every pull request.
Then jobs. We have one job, called test.
runs-on picks the machine: the latest Ubuntu runner.
And steps is the to-do list. Check out the

code. Install Node. Install dependencies. Run the
tests.

Fifteen lines, and every pull request now gets
tested
automatically.
Every step is one of two kinds.
A uses step pulls in an action — reusable

code someone already wrote. actions slash checkout,
at v4,

means: the checkout action, from the actions
organization, version
four. The with block passes it inputs.
A run step is plain shell. Whatever you'd type
in a terminal, you can put here. Use a
pipe character to write several lines.
Steps in a job share the same machine and
the same files. So step one checks out the
code, and step four can test it.
That shared workspace is what makes a job feel
like one continuous script.
So what actually happens when you push?
GitHub receives the push, and records an event.
It looks in dot github slash workflows — in
that exact commit — for workflows listening to push.
Each match becomes a workflow run, and its jobs
go into a queue.
A runner picks up a job. On hosted runners,
that's a brand new virtual machine, created just for
this job.

The runner downloads the actions, runs each step,
and
streams the logs back live.
When the job finishes, the machine is destroyed. And
a green check, or a red cross, appears next
to your commit.
You watch all of this in the Actions tab.
On the left, every run of every workflow. Click
one, and you see a graph of its jobs.
Click a job, and you get the live log
— every step, with its own timing, expandable line
by line.
The same result shows up on pull requests as
a status check.

With branch protection, you can make those checks
required.
The merge button stays locked until the tests pass.
That's the whole loop: a push, a run, a
verdict — right where the team works.
